frameworks.name: Skill Stacking Framework
frameworks.definition: A sequence where foundational skills (math, accounting) compound into specialized capabilities (tax, insurance, CFO readiness), enabling faster wealth creation than starting from scratch.

frameworks.name: Long-Term Greed Principle
frameworks.definition: Decision-making discipline where a founder assumes permanent ownership and evaluates every cost-cutting decision through a 10+ year lens, avoiding false savings that introduce long-term risk.

frameworks.name: Time Allocation Matrix
frameworks.definition: Classifying all work as either earning (work whose income is material to current cash needs) or learning (work whose knowledge gain is material to future earning power), ensuring all time falls into one of these two categories.

claims.text: Specialized skills are the only thing that appreciates over time and compounds reliably across economic cycles. Currency and market conditions change, but demand for good execution remains constant — if you are good, you will always have a place to provide value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Specialized competence is fundamentally different from asset ownership or capital because it is not devalued by inflation or economic collapse; market demand for good execution transcends currency regimes.

claims.text: Research is done through doing. You learn far more about viable opportunities by taking action in a domain than by planning in isolation; without operational baseline, you cannot recognize where opportunities actually exist.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Direct feedback from real market operations reveals constraints and leverage points that theoretical analysis cannot surface; you gain the insights to recognize opportunities only after you have worked in a domain.
bounded_by: Does not apply to domains requiring significant upfront capital or licensing (e.g., commercial aviation, nuclear energy)

claims.text: Y Combinator screening for founder success shows that past experience in the relevant industry — even tangential exposure like a parent's occupation — is a strong predictor. Industry knowledge, even if acquired accidentally or incidentally, reduces uncertainty.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Prior industry knowledge activates pattern recognition and reduces the decision space for what to try first; founders without any baseline operate with higher variance and longer time-to-insight.

claims.text: In any industry, opportunity increases monotonically with hierarchy level. A blender-tender at Smoothie King has minimal leverage; owning a location provides labor leverage; owning a franchise provides system and capital leverage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Leverage compounds at each organizational level because control over labor and systems multiplies the founder's effort; movement upward in hierarchy is movement from hands-on execution to leverage multiplication.

claims.text: The most durable industries are those that have persisted through economic downturns. Persistence signals structural profitability: only businesses with high gross margins survive extended downturns; low-margin businesses disappear.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: High margins provide cash reserves to absorb revenue volatility without forced cost-cutting that impairs long-term competitiveness; low-margin businesses have no cushion and become forced-sellers or closures during downturns.

claims.text: Insurance is a high-margin business model because customers pay thousands annually for coverage that may never occur; insurance companies' competitive advantage is in risk-valuation accuracy, not in service delivery.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Customers perceive insurance as pure cost (no immediate benefit), enabling insurers to capture the full probability-adjusted spread; the business model's profitability rests on statistical accuracy rather than operational excellence.

claims.text: The largest companies by net free cash flow (Exxon currently) sell commodities with minimal marginal cost (oil) at market-set prices, then optimize relentlessly on cost structure. Your goal as a founder is to drive cost down as much as possible without introducing risk that erodes long-term profitability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: If you commit to never exiting, cost optimization becomes aligned with long-term survival; cutting costs too aggressively (underpaying talent, degrading quality) introduces new risk categories that compound into larger losses over the business lifecycle.
bounded_by: Does not apply to venture-backed or exit-focused business models where timeline is constrained to 5-10 years

claims.text: The biggest mistake young entrepreneurs make is targeting millionaire status in 90 days when a guaranteed path exists: become a millionaire in a decade, but accept being non-millionaire for 9 of those 10 years. Most people will not sign that contract, so they chase shiny objects repeatedly instead.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The psychological cost of delayed gratification exceeds the mathematical benefit of compound growth in most people's decision-making; shiny-object chasing is a symptom of time-preference impatience, not information asymmetry.

claims.text: Business ownership is the highest-risk, highest-reward wealth-creation path. For founders with entrepreneurial tendencies, excellent sales ability offers a more reliable path: salespeople earning $200k-$300k annually are far more common than millionaire founders.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Sales skill is universally applicable across roles (selling investors, recruiting, persuading partners), making it a safer capital allocation than business ownership risk; the skill provides consistent returns rather than binary success/failure.

claims.text: Initial jobs are undervalued in skill acquisition. Most founders would benefit from assembling 3-4 adjacent jobs to build competency across multiple areas rather than seeking the 'perfect' role that never exists.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Skill compounds across domains; depth in accounting + tax + insurance = CFO capability. Sequential exposure to different function areas builds breadth that unattainable in a single early-stage role.

claims.text: When you're working, the opportunity cost of your time requires that you either be earning (the paycheck is material to your current cash position) or learning (the incremental knowledge is material to your future earning power). If your work time checks neither box, you are wasting your life.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: All time has opportunity cost; time not allocated to near-term cash generation or skill development accumulates to zero present value and zero future value — a double loss.

examples.text: Alex Hormozi's first job was as a blender tender at Smoothie King, which had virtually no leverage for growth. As a manager of the location, he would still have minimal growth potential. Owning the location provided labor leverage because he could supervise others. Owning a Smoothie King franchise multiplied that leverage through system replication and capital leverage.

Math skills enable accounting skills. Accounting skills enable tax skills. Tax skills enable insurance knowledge. Insurance knowledge enables CFO-level understanding. Each competency opens the next higher level because foundational knowledge removes the barrier to the next tier of complexity.

If your father owned a mechanic shop or was a mechanic, you probably know far more about cars than someone without that exposure. The exposed person has an information advantage, even if it seems obvious to them. Someone entering the space without that family knowledge starts from zero baseline.

Warren Buffett holds 25% of Berkshire Hathaway's value in cash (~$150 billion) despite inflation concerns. He has seen more economic cycles than younger entrepreneurs and is willing to wait for better opportunities rather than deploying capital into overheated markets. This willingness reflects experience-based patience, not fear.

practices.text: When evaluating whether to work at a job, ask whether the work is earning (paycheck is material) or learning (knowledge is material). If it is neither, decline or exit.
Build skill stacks sequentially rather than pursuing a single 'perfect' role. Assemble 3-4 adjacent positions to create compounding competency.

When considering business ownership, honestly assess whether you have entrepreneurial tendencies. If yes, recognize the high risk/reward structure. If no, build sales capability as a more reliable wealth path.
Look to long-standing industries (insurance, oil, JP Morgan) as signals of structural profitability and durable margins. New industries lack survival proof.
